Apple announced adjustments to App Tracking Transparency in Europe, and is now rolling out a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in the region. Here are the details.

Apple reforms business terms for EU app developers

Following an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator, Apple previously announced eight modifications to App Tracking Transparency in Europe.

The company has now announced a new commission structure set to take effect on October 1, which includes reducing the commission on external links to 15%, and replacing the controversial Core Technology Fee with a 5% Core Technology Commission.

This move comes just over a year after Apple announced major reforms to the EU App Store, when a complex set of rules was introduced — you can learn more about it here.

Below is Apple's statement:

Apple is also announcing new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative app payment options, and the distribution of apps through alternative app marketplaces or via the web.

The new terms are as follows:

For App Store apps completed via Apple in-app purchase, the commission is 26%. For the vast majority of developers — including those in the App Store Small Business Programme, Mini Apps Partner Programme, or Video Partner Programme, as well as subscriptions that auto-renew after the first year — the commission is 15%. For App Store apps using alternative payment processing, the commission is 20%. Developers in the programmes mentioned above will be eligible for a preferential rate of 10%. For App Store apps where transactions are completed by linking out to an external website from within the app, the commission is 15%. Developers in the programmes mentioned above will be eligible for a preferential rate of 10%. For apps distributed through alternative app marketplaces or via the web, Apple will charge a 5% Core Technology Commission.

Under the new terms, developers may also offer both Apple in-app purchase and alternative payment options within the app or via web links, provided they comply with Apple's 'Display Requirements' and maintain their chosen payment method for a period of 12 months.

Today's announcement also includes new child safety and alternative payment measures in the EU, including:

Apps in the Kids category on the App Store must not contain links that lead to websites for completing transactions, in order to reduce the risk of scams or fraud targeting children. For users under 18, all apps from the App Store that use alternative payment processing or link out to websites for transactions must incorporate a parental gate, requiring younger users to be accompanied by a parent or guardian before making a purchase. For users under 13, App Store apps must not link out to websites for transactions, in order to protect them from scams targeting young children.

Apple added that if EU member states require parental consent for digital activities by children aged 13 and above, 'these protections will be adjusted accordingly'.

Finally, Apple's latest announced changes also expand eligibility for operating alternative app marketplaces or distributing apps via the web.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Meeting a moderate level of financial stability as rated by Dun & Bradstreet. Being a publicly listed company or owned by one. Having venture capital funding from a recognised investment institution. Having completed a financial audit by a licensed accountant. Being a government body, educational institution, or non-profit organisation.

Apple noted that web distribution, currently available only in the EU, lacks the ongoing oversight provided by marketplace operators, which could allow bad actors to 'operate for extended periods before being detected, harming users'.

Accordingly, Apple said it will continue to require all apps distributed through alternative channels to go through its Notarisation process.

To learn more about today's announcements, click here.

Update: A European Commission spokesperson, responding to Bloomberg, said it welcomed Apple's changes, describing them as the result of 'close dialogue' with the company. The spokesperson added that the Commission would monitor Apple's implementation of the new terms.

What do you think of Apple's new rules in the EU? Let us know in the comments.
